newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's rebel jails "designed to provoke slow death".
newsitem.headline: Peru's rebel jails "designed to provoke slow death".

text.p: The parents of Lori Berenson, the American woman serving a life term in a prison high in Peru's Andes mountains, will not be able to see their daughter this week because of a new government ban on such visits.

Rhoda Berenson planned to deliver cooked chicken, vegetables or milk to her daughter, who has spent 23 1/2 hours a day in a tiny, ice-cold cell for over a year on terrorism charges in the 13,000-foot (4,000-metre) high Yanamayo prison.
The cell has no furniture and her toilet is a hole in the floor, where Berenson, 27, laboriously uses her swollen, deformed hands to pour water, her visitors have said.
After receiving "extremely insufficient" food for just over a year, Berenson, who grew up in New York City, is thinner, has laryngitis and suffers from digestive problems, her parents said.
"The system seems designed to provoke a slow death," her father, Mark Berenson, said. "You have to wonder how long someone can survive in these jails."
Berenson is one of hundreds of prisoners whose release is demanded by Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's resdience in Lima.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels claim their comrades -- and people like Berenson, whom they deny belongs to the group -- are held in jails "built with the aim of physically and psychologically destroying prisoners."

Last month the Berensons were allowed to visit their daughter for the first time since December 1995 when masked judges -- without hearing any cross-examination of government witnesses -- condemned her for allegedly plotting an MRTA takeover of Congress.
The parents saw her obvious weight loss despite her layers of sweaters and noted her "grotesque" hands due to circulation problems in the thin air up at the Andean city of Puno.
The U.S. State Department recognises Berenson is held in "very, very tough conditions."
"But she's luckier than those in Lima," Mark Berenson said, referring to the damp prisons that make their inmates vulnerable to chest infections.
Olinda Campos, the mother of MRTA leader, Victor Polay, told Reuters imprisonment at the country's most secure jail at Lima's port has turned her son into one of the "living dead."
"When I saw my son after his first fourteen months in prison, he was blind and weighed 30 kilos (66 pounds) less," Campos said.
Polay is kept 25 feet (eight metres) below ground with no access to natural light at a jail on the Pacific island of San Lorenzo before being transferred to port of Callao.
The navy base's eight cells, each six feet by nine feet (two metres by three metres), hold the leaders of the MRTA and Peru's larger guerrilla group, the Shining Path.
The cells' only light comes when jailors choose to uncover a six-inch (15-cm) diameter skylight in the concrete ceiling, according to local human rights groups.

Peru's National Coordinator for Human Rights claimed in a report that prisoners condemned on terrorism charges suffer "a regime that falls below the United Nations' requirement for the treatment of prisoners."
But President Alberto Fujimori -- who has refused to consider the hostage-takers' demand to release some 400 jailed rebels -- told reporters earlier this month Peru's jails have adequate standards.

"The prison conditions are provided in accordance with international standards and these are obeyed with as much rigour as anywhere else in the world," he said on a visit to a Lima prison holding MRTA rebels.

Fujimori admits "faceless" judges who speedily sentence accused rebels have made mistakes. While he has granted pardons to scores of prisoners wrongly condemned on terrorism charges, human rights groups claim up to 1,000 innocent people are still behind bars on such terrorism charges.
Fujimori has no intention of changing the system.
Francisco Soberon, head of local human rights group, APRODEH, said Fujimori was right to have introduced stricter treatment for rebels but believed the system had gone too far.
"Previously the prisons became ideological centres, with painted slogans and subversives wearing uniforms and bandanas," he said.
"But now the torture has to be abolished and the laws must be made more flexible."
